title: He says that…: reported speech
topic: reported speech in the present and the past
why: Now that the learner has mastered the imperfect, the pluperfect and the conditional, they can report what other people say: dice que + same tense, dijo que + tenses shifting back, questions with si and commands with que + subjunctive. It's the second-to-last lesson of level B1, right before the big review.

Dice que…: reporting in the present

To report what someone says, Spanish works like English: a verb like decir, then que. When the reporting verb is in the present, the tenses don't change; only the persons change (yo becomes él, mi becomes su…).

What's saidWhat's reported
«Estoy cansada.»Ana dice que está cansada.
«Mañana iré al médico.»Dice que mañana irá al médico.
«He comprado las entradas.»Dice que ha comprado las entradas.
«Mi hermano vive en Bilbao.»Dice que su hermano vive en Bilbao.

The que is required: English can drop “that” (“Ana says she's tired”), but Spanish never can: never “Dice está cansada.”

Questions

A yes/no question is reported with si (“if, whether”); an open question keeps its question word, with its written accent.

«¿Vienes al cine?» → Me pregunta si voy al cine.“Are you coming to the movies?” → He asks me if I'm going to the movies.
«¿Dónde vives?» → Me pregunta dónde vivo.“Where do you live?” → He asks me where I live.

Commands and requests

Watch out, trap: English says “he tells me to come,” with an infinitive, but Spanish says me dice que venga, with the present subjunctive you've known since unit 15.

«Ven a las ocho.» → Me dice que venga a las ocho.“Come at eight.” → He tells me to come at eight.

Preguntar is for asking a question (Me pregunta si…); pedir is for asking for something or a favor (Me pide que lo ayude). English uses “ask” for both.

", "

Dijo que…: tenses shift back

When the reporting verb is in the past (dijo, me contó, explicó, me preguntó), the tenses shift back one step, just like in English: “He said he was tired.”

Direct speechReported speech in the past
present: «Estoy cansado.»imperfect: Dijo que estaba cansado.
perfecto: «He perdido las llaves.»pluperfect: Dijo que había perdido las llaves.
indefinido: «Llegué tarde.»pluperfect: Dijo que había llegado tarde. (in speech also: que llegó tarde)
future: «Te llamaré.»conditional: Dijo que me llamaría.
imperfect: «Antes vivía en Cádiz.»no change: Dijo que antes vivía en Cádiz.
conditional: «Me gustaría ir.»no change: Dijo que le gustaría ir.

Questions follow the same rule: «¿Tienes hambre?» → Me preguntó si tenía hambre.

Commands reported in the past

The command becomes the imperfect subjunctive, the form you saw with si tuviera. For now, you just need to recognize it:

«Llámame.» → Me dijo que lo llamara.“Call me.” → He told me to call him.
«Compra pan.» → Mi madre me pidió que comprara pan.“Buy bread.” → My mother asked me to buy bread.

If what was said is still true as you speak, you can keep the present: Me dijo que vive en Toledo (he still lives there). When in doubt, shift the tenses back: Me dijo que vivía en Toledo is always correct.

", "

Reference words that change

When you report words later or somewhere else, words for time and place change too, as in English (“tomorrow” becomes “the next day”).

Direct speechReported speechEnglish
hoyaquel día, ese díathat day
mañanaal día siguientethe next day
ayerel día anteriorthe day before
la semana que vienela semana siguientethe following week
ahoraentonces, en ese momentothen, at that moment
aquíallíthere
este, estaese, esa / aquel, aquellathat

In the same way, venir and traer can become ir and llevar when the person reporting is no longer in the same place.

A complete example

Lunes: «Mañana iré a tu casa y llevaré la tarta.»Monday: “Tomorrow I'll come to your place and bring the cake.”
Viernes: Elena me dijo que al día siguiente iría a mi casa y llevaría la tarta.Friday: Elena told me that the next day she would come to my place and bring the cake.

Reporting verbs

decir (to say, to tell), contar (to tell, to recount), explicar (to explain), comentar (to remark), añadir (to add), contestar or responder (to answer), prometer (to promise), preguntar (to ask a question), pedir (to ask for something).

In speech, Spaniards often add a que before a reported question: Me preguntó que si quería venir. It's very common, but in writing, go with Me preguntó si quería venir.
